tldr: We propose a method where a vision-language critic diagnoses why a robot policy failed, compiles these diagnoses into "generation programs" that recreate the difficulties and "training programs" that help overcome them, and stores them in a shared memory. This enables the simulation data engine and the robot action policy to adapt and co-evolve. As a result, the task success rate in unseen, out-of-distribution (OOD) environments jumped from 5.3% to 27.6% (and up to 42.1%).
hero_caption: An overview of the CoDA framework. A coding agent data generator creates scenes, while a VLM diagnoses policy execution failures and records them in a shared memory. The memory automatically synthesizes generation programs and reward shaping programs via Text2potential, co-evolving policy learning and data generation in a closed loop.
overview:
Simulation is an invaluable data source for robot learning. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have made it possible to automatically generate diverse scenes and tasks. However, generating a physically plausible environment is very different from generating one that actually helps overcome the policy's current weaknesses. Prior methods merely randomized predefined parameter ranges or adjusted generation ratios based solely on overall task success rates. They failed to directly reflect learning progress—namely, why the policy failed and how best to teach it.

To bridge this gap, the authors propose CoDA, a framework where a simulation data engine and an action policy co-evolve. A vision-language model (VLM) critic diagnoses robot failure trajectories to identify failure factors (task, spatial configuration, object attributes) and the motion phase where the failure occurred (approach, grasp, etc.). These diagnoses are stored in a three-layer shared memory (episodic, semantic, procedural) and automatically compiled into environment generation programs that recreate weaknesses and training programs (Text2potential) that provide auxiliary rewards via staged potential functions.

Evaluated on four manipulation task families and the LIBERO-Pro benchmark, out-of-distribution (OOD) success jumped from 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning to 27.6%, climbing to 42.1% over extended rounds. Furthermore, the accumulated memory transferred effectively to a completely different robot policy model zero-shot.
contributions: Established the CoDA framework that co-evolves the environment generation engine and action policy in a closed loop, dynamically adapting generated environments according to the policy's learning progress.

Introduced a three-layer shared heterogeneous memory that compiles failure diagnoses into generation programs recreating weaknesses and training programs aiding mastery, systematically managing difficulty modes and learning progress.

Proposed Text2potential, which converts failure diagnoses into simulator-state-based staged potential functions, offering dense scaffolding for action-chunk value learning without altering the optimal policy.
Substantially improved out-of-distribution generalization and demonstrated zero-shot transfer of the accumulated memory across task families and to distinct policy models (such as OpenVLA).

sections.heading: Moving from Just Generating Environments to Targeted Co-Evolution
sections.summary: Generative simulation is automating the construction of physical environments, but choosing which environments offer true learning value and what supervision to provide remained unresolved. CoDA introduces a closed-loop framework where a data generator and an action policy co-evolve through a shared memory that tracks failure diagnoses and learning progress.
sections.details:
In robot manipulation learning, building simulation environments has long been the primary bottleneck. Designing tasks, selecting assets, arranging layouts, and writing reward functions all required manual effort. Modern generative AI has begun relieving this bottleneck, as code generation agents can autonomously produce scenes and tasks.

Yet this brings a new hurdle: which environment should be built next, and what supervisory signal best facilitates learning from it? Existing data engines mostly rely on domain randomization over human-specified ranges, heuristic scene repair for physical validity, or allocating generation budgets based on overall task success rates. However, these risk wasting compute on environments the policy has already mastered or those far too difficult to learn from at the moment.

This is where CoDA comes in. CoDA introduces a shared memory between the simulation data engine and the action policy, forming a closed loop. When the policy fails in an environment, a vision-language model (VLM) critic pinpoints the root cause. From this diagnosis, it automatically synthesizes environment generation code that recreates the weakness and training code that breaks the task into subgoals with dense potential rewards. By tracking learning progress, the system focuses environment generation and updates on difficulty patterns with the highest room for improvement.

In experiments, CoDA achieved a 27.6% out-of-distribution (OOD) success rate (unseen objects and configurations) compared to 5.3% after supervised fine-tuning (SFT). It surpassed a success-rate-guided closed-loop baseline (18.1%) with the same generation budget by 9.5 percentage points, and reached 42.1% across extended cycles.

sections.heading: Fusing Agentic Simulation Generation with Curriculum Learning
sections.summary: This section surveys recent data engine research autonomously synthesizing 3D assets and scenes, alongside curriculum learning and reinforcement learning paradigms that adaptively regulate difficulty. CoDA's novelty lies in bridging them directly via failure diagnoses structured by scene factors and motion phases.
sections.details:
Related work largely splits into two research lines.

The first is agentic asset and scene synthesis. Works like RoboGen, RoboTwin 2.0, and SimFoundry leverage LLMs to automatically generate tasks, scene layouts, and articulated objects. However, these systems lack mechanisms to dynamically adjust generation content in response to the policy's real-time learning progress (learning curves).

The second is curriculum learning and policy improvement. Methods like POET co-evolve agents and environment parameters, Eureka prompts LLMs to write reward functions, and other works fine-tune action chunks using Q-learning. However, these rely on sparse success metrics (0 or 1) or require human inspection to prompt failure descriptions.

CoDA integrates the strengths of both lines. By grounding diagnoses in both scene factors (task, spatial configuration, object attributes) and robot motion phases (approach, grasp, transport, etc.), it simultaneously provides precise intervention directives to the generation engine and fine-grained reward shaping to policy learning, distinctly setting it apart from prior work.

sections.heading: How the Co-Evolution Loop Operates via Shared Memory and Text2potential
sections.summary: Scenes are expressed as structured programs, and VLM failure diagnoses are aggregated into a three-layer memory: episodic, semantic, and procedural. Furthermore, Text2potential automatically constructs intermediate potential functions from points of failure, accelerating action-chunk value learning without altering the underlying optimal policy.
sections.details:
CoDA consists of a data generator $\mathcal{G}$, an action policy $\pi_{\theta}$, a VLM critic $\mathcal{C}$, and a shared memory $\mathcal{M}$.

### 3.1 Seed Generation and Factorized Scene Representation
First, tasks with verifiable success predicates $\nu$ are sampled from an object pool. Crucially, each environment is managed as a factorized program $s = (\tau, \sigma, \alpha)$:
- $\tau$ (Task factors): instructions, initial/terminal state conditions, and success predicates.
- $\sigma$ (Spatial layout factors): object poses, support relations, and occlusion levels.
- $\alpha$ (Intrinsic object attributes): shape, scale, mass, friction, appearance, etc.
Equipping the SDK with functions to resample each factor independently enables controlled intervention experiments, such as making only spatial layouts harder while keeping all other conditions identical.

### 3.2 Three-Layer Shared Heterogeneous Memory
The memory adopts a three-layer architecture inspired by human cognition:
- **Episodic layer**: Stores chronological logs of executed scene programs, success predicates $\nu$, success rates, learning progress, and VLM failure diagnoses $\psi = (\delta, p, c, e)$ (factor $\delta$, phase $p$, explanation $c$, and supporting evidence $e$).
- **Semantic layer**: Clusters episodes into reusable "difficulty modes," such as an obstacle placed in front of the target. Each mode is weighted by its current difficulty (low success rate) and importance (learning progress potential).
- **Procedural layer**: Compiles difficulty modes into two executable programs: environment generation code $\Omega$ and training code $\Phi$.

### 3.3 Memory-Guided Scene Generation and Counterfactual Verification
The generation budget is allocated across modes using an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) rule that balances difficulty and learning progress. A standout feature here is "counterfactual experimentation." When a specific factor (e.g., spatial layout) is diagnosed as the cause of failure, the engine creates both a target batch varying that factor and a control batch varying an unrelated factor. Only when the target batch shows significantly lower success is the diagnosis verified as a true bottleneck and registered in the procedural layer.

### 3.4 Text2potential: Automatic Staged Potential Rewards from Diagnoses
For long-horizon tasks, sparse success rewards $\nu$ (0 or 1) slow reinforcement learning. Text2potential addresses this by segmenting the task into $m$ subgoals at the diagnosed failure phase $p$. It synthesizes a staged potential $\Phi(s)$ combining completion predicates $\text{done}_k(s)$ and progress potentials $\varphi_k(s) \in [0, 1)$ for each subgoal, evaluated directly on the simulator's internal state.

### 3.5 Action-Chunk Value Learning and Policy Updates
Policy learning employs potential-based reward shaping: $\tilde{r}_t = r_t + \beta [\gamma \Phi(s_{t+1}) - \Phi(s_{t})]$. Because actions are processed in chunks of length $h$, evaluating the potential difference between chunk endpoints $s_t$ and $s_{t+h}$ provides dense guidance. Theoretically, this form of shaping preserves the original task's optimal policy.
Policy parameters $\pi_\theta$ are updated via Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) to imitate chunks prioritized by the value critic $Q_\phi$. This allows stable weighted updates even for diffusion or flow-matching action policies.

captions.F1: Detailed architecture of CoDA. The data generator on the left constructs factorized scenes ($\tau, \sigma, \alpha$). A VLM critic diagnoses failures from policy rollouts (bottom right). Routed through the central three-layer shared memory, diagnoses feed into reward design via Text2potential (top right) and next-round generation programs (top left).

sections.heading: Leaps in Out-of-Distribution Generalization and Cross-Policy Knowledge Transfer
sections.summary: Evaluated across four manipulation task families and the LIBERO-Pro benchmark, CoDA dramatically improved out-of-distribution (OOD) success rates. Experiments also validated the impact of different VLM critics, the training acceleration from Text2potential, and the zero-shot transferability of the accumulated memory to a distinct policy backbone.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on four manipulation task families (pick-and-place, articulated door opening, packing, and stacking/insertion) and the challenging LIBERO-Pro benchmark. The base policy was a 3B flow-matching model, $\pi_{0.5}$, fine-tuned with LoRA.

### Main Results and Out-of-Distribution Generalization
On the four task families, the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baseline achieved only a 5.3% average success rate under out-of-distribution (OOD: unseen objects, layouts, and categories) settings, whereas CoDA achieved 27.6% (Table 1). CoDA significantly outperformed the closed-loop baseline guided solely by task success rate (18.1%) and a memory-ablated variant (19.2%). Compared to domain randomization (7.9%) and uniform generation (8.5%), CoDA delivered more than a threefold gain. Extending the co-evolution cycle to 15 rounds increased success continuously to 42.1%.

### Robustness to Perturbations on LIBERO-Pro
On LIBERO-Pro, the models were evaluated under position perturbations (Pos) and instruction perturbations (Task) (Table 2). The initial checkpoint struggled severely, scoring 25% under position perturbations and 1% under instruction perturbations. After 15 rounds of CoDA training, success jumped dramatically to 84% and 76%, respectively, substantially exceeding the strong prior method ASPIRE (77% and 67%). Performance on standard LIBERO remained high (97.4%), confirming that generalizability was gained without catastrophic forgetting.

### Impact of Text2potential and Critic Ablations
Evaluating reward shaping with Text2potential (Table 4) revealed that while sparse success rewards required 31,000 updates to reach 25% OOD success, CoDA reached it in 21,000 updates, cutting training steps by about 32%. Final performance also increased from 22.3% to 27.6%.
Swapping the diagnostic VLM across GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 5, InternVL3-78B, and Qwen3-VL-235B (Table 3) consistently produced 24.9%–27.6% success rates, comfortably surpassing the 18.1% success-rate-guided baseline. This demonstrates that the framework is robust and not tied to any single VLM.

captions.F3: Execution snapshots of robot policies on LIBERO-Pro and generated vegetable cooking tasks. Even under initial position offsets (5 cm to 43 cm shifts), size changes, and asset substitutions, the policy succeeds by accurately following the subgoal sequence learned through Text2potential (grasp $\rightarrow$ transport $\rightarrow$ place).

sections.heading: A New Paradigm for Jointly Nurturing Data Generation and Action Policies
sections.summary: This section summarizes the efficacy of CoDA in co-evolving environment generation and policy learning in a closed loop around a shared memory. Using failure diagnoses to automatically generate environments and dense guidance provides a powerful stepping stone toward autonomous training of robot foundation models.
sections.details:
This work proposed CoDA, directly linking simulation data generation engines with robot policy learning through a shared heterogeneous memory. By using a VLM to diagnose where the policy struggles and translating those findings into weakness-recreating generation programs and staged potential functions, CoDA sustains an automated loop of efficient, systematic data collection and policy improvement.

Experiments confirmed superior generalization to unseen environments, significantly accelerated training, and knowledge transfer across task suites and policy architectures. It charts a clear path from manually diagnosing failures and crafting environments to an era where AI-to-AI interaction autonomously organizes learning curricula.

sections.heading: Appendix: Program Lifting Transfer and In-Depth Validations
sections.summary: Details on "program lifting" to transfer generation programs across task families via symbolic roles, experimental results transferring accumulated memory to another policy model (OpenVLA), and physical validation checks.
sections.details:
### Transferring Generation Programs to Heterogeneous Tasks (Lifting)
To apply environment generation programs learned in one task to another, CoDA describes scene conditions using symbolic roles ("target", "obstacle", "support fixture") and geometric constraints rather than concrete object IDs. Matching and binding these roles to a new scene's symbol table quickly builds effective challenge environments with lower LLM token consumption than generating code from scratch. In experiments, this achieved roughly 1.7x higher learning progress efficiency (60.3% vs. 35.8%) compared to scratch generation.

### Reusing Memory Across Heterogeneous Policy Backbones
Interestingly, the shared memory collected and accumulated using $\pi_{0.5}$ (3B) was frozen and applied without generating any new environments to train an entirely different policy model, OpenVLA-OFT (7B) (Table 7). OpenVLA's OOD success rate surged from 3.8% to 21.1%. This confirms that the extracted difficulty modes and subgoal decompositions capture universal task knowledge rather than policy-specific weights.

### Generation Quality and Rejecting Diagnoses via Counterfactuals
The generator achieved an 88.9% physical validity pass rate, outperforming random generation (71.3%) in scene quality (Table 8). Furthermore, 18.2% of VLM failure diagnoses were rejected by counterfactual experiments (where perturbing an unrelated factor yielded no change in failure rate). This filtering raised agreement with human annotators from 73.6% to 82.4%, proving that experimental verification is vital for filtering out LLM hallucinations.

captions.F5: Examples of diverse scene variations autonomously generated by CoDA. In tasks such as tool sorting and serving board preparation, the system systematically applies spatial shifts, object resizing, and asset replacement from seed environments without physical breakdowns.

takeaways: Merely generating "physically valid environments" at random is insufficient; an environment generation loop that pinpoints and responds to the policy's current weaknesses (failure phases and factors) is essential.
The three-layer memory design—compiling failure diagnoses into both recreation programs and training programs (potential rewards)—is remarkably scalable.
Rather than trusting VLM diagnoses blindly, experimental verification using factor-isolated counterfactual batches reliably filters out misdiagnoses and hallucinations.

Accumulated difficulty modes and curriculum programs are highly generalizable, transferring zero-shot to completely different policy backbones (from $\pi_{0.5}$ to OpenVLA) without requiring additional environment generation.
limitations: Scene generation, failure diagnosis, and potential synthesis all rely heavily on large foundation models (such as GPT-5.5), resulting in notable API inference costs and iterative simulation compute overhead.

Evaluations are confined to MuJoCo simulation environments (four task families and LIBERO-Pro); verifying transfer to real robot hardware (Real-to-Sim-to-Real) with complex contact dynamics and sensor noise remains future work.
Subtle simulation glitches or unnatural object dynamics that slip past physical sanity checks might still elude detection by counterfactual experiments.
